newsitem.title: USA: Pakistan, India cotton losing market share -- USDA.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan, India cotton losing market share -- USDA.

text.p: Government initiatives encouraging the use of synthetic materials will limit cotton's share of the fiber market in Pakistan and India, according to U.S. Agriculture Department.
The textile industry is the largest industry in both countries, and Pakistan and India are among the world's major producers, consumers and exporters of raw cotton.

"The outlook for the two countries indicates continued growth in cotton production and consumption, although cotton's share of total fiber is expected to decline," Ronald Roberson of the USDA's foreign agricultural service, said.
Roberson was speaking at the annual Beltwide Cotton Conferences here.

In Pakistan, the government reduced to five percent a regulatory duty of 15 percent for polyester imports and 10 percent for viscose imports. A 10 percent regulatory duty on raw materials for manufacturing polyester was also lifted.

The government also moved to liberalize cotton trade over the past two years, Roberson said. But overall, "as government policies encourage the use of man-made fibers, the growth in mill use of cotton is expected to be slower than the growth in the overall textile sector."

Output, meantime, has been battered by pests and disease over the past several years. Yields in most areas are reported to be 10 percent to 33 percent lower in 1996, from a year ago. USDA estimates Pakistan's 1996/97 crop at 6.8 million bales, down 1.4 million bales from last year.

As in Pakistan, India's government is promoting increased use of synthetic fiber and has set a goal of raising synthetic fiber share to 50 percent from a current 30 percent. The import duty for polyester fiber was lowered in July to 30 percent from 45 percent, Roberson said.

Despite a projected cotton crop at a near-record of 12.3 million bales in 1996/97, strong yields and improved quality, the growth in mill use of cotton is seen slowing as a result of the government initiatives, he said.
"With the removal of textile quotas by the year 2005, India is expected to increase its production of apparel and other finished products," Roberson said.
